_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: WinMain and the window handle (HWND)
rungs.builds: main from Your first C program (Phase 1), Structs and the dot operator and Pointers: & and * (Phase 3.5), Function pointers (Phase 3.75) and Preprocessor switches (Phase 4.5).
rungs.why: A console program just runs. A window has to be created, and Windows hands you back a handle for it: the HWND. Every later call (show it, draw on it, close it) needs that ticket. This is the boilerplate you fill in once per game.

parts: A window is something you ask for

A console program owns its text and just prints. A window belongs to Windows. You fill in a form describing a kind of window (a WNDCLASS), register it, ask CreateWindowEx for one window of that kind, and Windows hands back an HWND, the handle you quote in every later call. Then a loop keeps the program alive. That's the whole file; the rest is detail.
The type names are typedefs

Win32 renamed ordinary C types with typedef, just as you named your structs in Structs and the dot operator. UINT is unsigned int. DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned long. LPSTR is char *. BOOL is a plain int, not C's bool. WPARAM, LPARAM and LRESULT are integers as wide as a pointer, so 8 bytes on x64. Hover over any of them in VS Code to see what it really is.

The prefixes on names tell you the type: h is a handle (hInst, hwnd), lp is a pointer (the "long" is left over from 16-bit Windows), lpsz is a pointer to a string ending in '\0', lpfn is a pointer to a function. The w and l in wp and lp once meant "word" and "long"; today both are pointer-sized.
A handle is a pointer you can't see through

windows.h declares HWND as a pointer to a little struct that has nothing useful in it. The real window data lives inside Windows, where you can't reach it. So you can store an HWND, compare it with NULL and pass it back, but never look inside. That's on purpose: Windows can change its insides without breaking your program. HWND, HBRUSH and HDC are different pointer types, so passing a brush where a window belongs makes MSVC warn, and /WX stops the build.
CALLBACK and the bare function name

CALLBACK and WINAPI are #define macros for a calling convention, the rule for how arguments get passed. On x64 there's only one convention and the compiler ignores them, but keep them: 32-bit builds need them. wc.lpfnWndProc = WindowProc; has no brackets, so it stores the function's address, exactly as in Function pointers. The field's type, WNDPROC, is a typedef for that function shape.
CreateWindowEx is two functions

There's no function called CreateWindowEx. Windows has CreateWindowExA, which takes char strings, and CreateWindowExW, which takes wide strings. windows.h uses #ifdef UNICODE to point the plain name at one of them: Preprocessor switches again. build.bat doesn't define UNICODE, so you get the A versions and "GameWindow" works. RegisterClass, DefWindowProc and MessageBox work the same way. Visual Studio projects define UNICODE, which is why copied code often writes L"GameWindow".
Mistakes and MSVC notes

• A global or static starts at zero, so g_hwnd would be NULL even without = NULL (Static locals and globals). A local doesn't: without = {0}, wc is full of garbage and RegisterClass can fail.
  • The class name in RegisterClass and CreateWindowEx must match exactly, or CreateWindowEx returns NULL.
  • Both calls report failure through their return value. Check it while you're learning.

An unused parameter is warning C4100 at /W4, so /WX stops the build. The (void)hPrev; line "uses" it. build.bat's /external:W0 keeps windows.h's own warnings quiet.

walk: HWND is a “handle to a window”: a pointer to a struct you can’t see inside. You never look in it; you just hand it back in later calls. NULL means “no window yet”. A static global starts at zero anyway; the = NULL just says so.
Windows will call this function for every event on the window. For now it passes everything to Windows’ default handling. The window procedure fills it in.
WinMain is main for a windowed program. Windows passes in hInst (this program’s own handle) and nShow (how the window should first appear).
The other two parameters are unused. Under /W4 /WX an unused parameter is a warning turned into an error, so “use” them with a (void) cast.
A form describing a kind of window. It’s a local, so without = {0} every field would be garbage. This zeroes them all, so you only fill in the ones you care about.
The important field: the address of your callback. No brackets after WindowProc, so this is its address, as in Function pointers. Windows rings this number whenever something happens.
Hands the form to Windows under the name “GameWindow”. No UNICODE is defined, so RegisterClass means RegisterClassA, the plain char version.
CreateWindowEx builds the window from that class name and returns its HWND. 800 and 600 are the size. The window exists now but is not visible.
Named numbers: WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW means a normal window with a title bar, border and minimise/maximise/close buttons. CW_USEDEFAULT twice means “let Windows pick the position”.
Makes it appear. Without this line the window exists but nobody can see it.

The message loop keeps the program alive: GetMessage waits for the next message, then TranslateMessage and DispatchMessage pass it on to WindowProc. It gets its own concept, The message loop and PeekMessage. Without it, WinMain would end and the window would vanish at once.
rungs.model: Mental model: registering a class is filling in a form for a type of window. CreateWindowEx is ordering one from that form, and the HWND is the claim ticket. Every later call says “about window number…” using that ticket.

check.q: You delete the ShowWindow line and run the program. What happens?
opts: The window appears anyway, because CreateWindowEx makes it visible
The program refuses to compile, because ShowWindow is required
Nothing is visible, but the program keeps running
The program exits straight away, because there is no window to show
check.hint: CreateWindowEx builds the window. What does ShowWindow add?
check.why: CreateWindowEx makes the window but, without the WS_VISIBLE style, hides it. ShowWindow is what puts it on screen. The message loop still runs, so the process sits there with nothing to look at.

miss.0: This style of CreateWindowEx call doesn’t include WS_VISIBLE, so the window stays hidden until ShowWindow.
miss.1: ShowWindow is just a function call. Leaving it out compiles fine.
miss.3: The program ends when the message loop ends, not when the window is missing. GetMessage keeps waiting.

tryit.task: Change the title bar text and the window size to 640 by 480.

qa: Why doesn’t clicking X end the program?
X destroys the window, but nothing tells the message loop to stop, so the process keeps running with no window. The window procedure fixes this with WM_DESTROY.
Why WinMain and not main?

Windows hands a GUI program things a console program never needs, like its own instance handle. The C runtime sets everything up and then calls your WinMain, the way it calls main in a console program.
What are CW_USEDEFAULT and WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW?
Named numbers. The first means “let Windows pick the position”. The second is several style flags joined into one number; Combining flags with | and & shows how.
I don’t know half these type names (LRESULT, WPARAM, HINSTANCE). Is that okay?

Yes. They are typedefs for ordinary types: HINSTANCE and HWND are handles, WPARAM is a pointer-sized number. Win32 dates from the early 1990s and named everything twice. Understanding about a fifth of this file on the first read is normal.
Can I print an HWND?
Yes, with %p, like any pointer: 16 hex digits on x64. The number means nothing to you, though. It only matters to Windows.
rungs.bridge: You can create and show a window. Next: Linking libraries, the two words this program needs on the build line before it will link at all.

rungs.title: Linking libraries (user32.lib, gdi32.lib)
rungs.builds: Linker errors (LNK2019) from Phase 3.75, and the build.bat FLAGS and SOURCES lines. The window from WinMain and the window handle is the program you’re linking.
rungs.why: windows.h only declares CreateWindowEx and FillRect, like a menu. The real code lives in Windows’ own libraries. If you don’t tell the linker which ones, the window you just wrote dies with LNK2019 even though every line compiled.

parts: Declared isn't defined

windows.h only declares CreateWindowExA: its name and shape. The code is inside Windows, in DLLs such as user32.dll and gdi32.dll. To call it, the linker needs an import library like user32.lib: a small file that lists what the DLL contains, so the linker can write “fetch this from user32.dll at start-up” into your .exe. The .lib is used when you build, the DLL when you run. King tells the same story with the maths library, which some systems make you ask for by name.
Which library?

Look the function up on Microsoft Learn. The Requirements table at the bottom of its page names the header, the library and the DLL: CreateSolidBrush says Gdi32.lib. Windows, messages and input are user32.lib; brushes and bitmaps are gdi32.lib. The window from WinMain and the window handle only needs user32.lib, but put both on build.bat's cl line now, before you start drawing.
Reading the error

The compile step passes, because the header declared everything. The link step fails with LNK2019, and the name it quotes is __imp_CreateSolidBrush: __imp_ means “the slot imported from a DLL”. Strip it and look the rest up. Older posts show names like _WindowProc@16; that's 32-bit decoration, and x64 has none.
MSVC notes

MSVC can also take the library from the source file: #pragma comment(lib, "gdi32.lib"). Misspell comment and MSVC warns C4068 (unknown pragma), because compilers skip pragmas they don't know. /WX makes that error C2220. Misspell the library name instead and the linker stops because it can't open the file. This course keeps libraries on the build line, where you can see them all.

rungs.code:
REM build.bat: add the Windows libraries to the cl line (REM starts a comment)
cl %FLAGS% %SOURCES% user32.lib gdi32.lib /Fe:game.exe

REM Once you draw, leaving gdi32.lib off compiles, then fails to link:
REM   win32_window.obj : error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol
REM       __imp_CreateSolidBrush referenced in function WindowProc
REM   game.exe : fatal error LNK1120: 2 unresolved externals
REM (the count is how many gdi32 functions your file calls)
REM
REM Leave user32.lib off and the same error names a user32 function:
REM   unresolved external symbol __imp_CreateWindowExA
walk: build.bat’s cl line, with two library names added. user32.lib covers windows, messages and input (CreateWindowEx, GetMessage, FillRect). gdi32.lib covers drawing objects (CreateSolidBrush, DeleteObject, BitBlt). Your first window only needs user32, but list both now.
Missing library: the compile step passes, because the header declared the function. The link step fails. You’ll see this one once Drawing with GDI makes a brush.
“Unresolved external symbol”: the linker was told to call a function and can’t find its code. Linker errors (LNK2019) showed the same error for your own files.

Strip the __imp_ (“imported from a DLL”) and you can read it: CreateSolidBrush. It’s a GDI function, so the fix is gdi32.lib. On x64 there’s no leading underscore and no @4 on the end; those only appear in 32-bit builds.
The summary line: it counts how many symbols were missing. Fix the first one and the rest usually go too.
rungs.model: Mental model: windows.h is the menu, the .lib files are the kitchens. The menu lists CreateWindowEx, but the linker needs to know which kitchen (user32 or gdi32) actually cooks it.

check.q: Your build fails with: unresolved external symbol __imp_CreateSolidBrush referenced in function WindowProc. What is the fix?
opts: Add an include for wingdi.h at the top of the file
Add user32.lib to the cl line in build.bat
Add gdi32.lib to the cl line in build.bat
Rename CreateSolidBrush, because it is misspelled
check.hint: Which step reports missing code: the compiler or the linker? Then ask which library holds drawing objects like brushes.
check.why: A linker error with the function’s name means the code was declared but not found. CreateSolidBrush is a GDI (drawing) function, so it lives in gdi32.lib. windows.h already pulls in the GDI header, which is why it compiled.

miss.0: The header is already included through windows.h. A missing declaration would be a compile error, not LNK2019.
miss.1: user32.lib holds window and input functions. Brushes are GDI, so they live in gdi32.lib.
miss.3: A misspelled name would be caught by the compiler. LNK2019 means the name was fine but the code wasn’t linked.

tryit.task: Write build.bat’s cl line for the window, with both libraries.

qa: Is there a way to put this in the source file instead?
Yes: #pragma comment(lib, "user32.lib") in MSVC. It’s handy for small tests. This course keeps the libraries on the build line so build.bat shows everything the program needs.
Why did gcc/MinGW use -luser32 instead?
Different compiler, same idea: -luser32 -lgdi32 tell its linker which libraries to use. You only need the cl form.
Older answers online show _WindowProc@16 and __imp__CreateSolidBrush@4. Why don’t I see those?

That’s 32-bit Windows, where the compiler decorates names with an underscore and the number of argument bytes. Your build is x64, which has one calling convention and no decoration, so you see WindowProc and __imp_CreateSolidBrush.
Does the .lib end up inside my .exe?
Only a small table from it. The real code stays in user32.dll and gdi32.dll, which every copy of Windows already has, so your .exe stays small.
rungs.bridge: You can build the window. Next: Combining flags with | and &, the C behind WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW and RGB.

rungs.title: Combining flags with | and &
rungs.builds: Named constants with #define (Phase 3), Comparisons, &&, || and ! (Phase 2.5), and How big a number can be (Phase 2).
rungs.why: Windows packs a dozen yes-or-no options into one number: the window’s border, title bar and buttons are all bits in WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW. Your game can do the same with a player’s status: alive, shielded, poisoned, all in one unsigned int. Reading Win32 code means reading | and &.

parts: One number, many switches

An unsigned int is 32 bits, and each bit can be a yes or no. Give each bit a name and one variable holds 32 separate switches: alive, jumping, shielded, poisoned. That's a set of bit flags. Windows uses them everywhere, so you need to read them before the next concepts.
Making the flags with <<

1u << n shifts a 1 left by n places, giving a number with only bit n on: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Each flag is a different power of two, so no two share a bit. You'll also see them written in hex: 0x1, 0x2, 0x4, 0x8. C17 has no binary literals; C23 adds 0b1000, so you may meet it in newer code. >> shifts the other way. Use unsigned: shifting a 1 into the top bit of a signed int is undefined behaviour.
Set, clear, toggle, test

flags |= FLAG_SHIELD;                // set: turn that bit on
flags &= ~FLAG_SHIELD;               // clear: turn it off
flags ^= FLAG_JUMPING;               // toggle: flip it
if ((flags & FLAG_POISONED) != 0)    // test: is it on?

| gives a 1 wherever either side has one. & gives a 1 only where both do, so it works like a stencil: flags & FLAG_POISONED keeps that one bit and zeroes the rest. ~ flips every bit, so ~FLAG_SHIELD is a mask with every bit on except the shield. AND with it and only the shield goes.
The two traps

Precedence. flags & FLAG_POISONED != 0 looks right but reads as flags & (FLAG_POISONED != 0), because != binds tighter than &. That's flags & 1, which tests the alive bit instead. Always bracket the &, or drop the != 0 and write if (flags & FLAG_POISONED).

& is not &&. The logical operators from Comparisons, &&, || and ! only ever give 0 or 1. FLAG_ALIVE || FLAG_SHIELD is 1, not 5, and flags && FLAG_SHIELD is true whenever any flag at all is set. Both compile without a word.
Where Win32 uses this

WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW is six window styles joined with |: WS_OVERLAPPED, WS_CAPTION, WS_SYSMENU, WS_THICKFRAME, WS_MINIMIZEBOX and WS_MAXIMIZEBOX. Want a window the player can't resize? Take two out: WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW & ~(WS_THICKFRAME | WS_MAXIMIZEBOX).

Join flags with |, never +. A bit that's already on stays on with |, but + carries it into the next bit. WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW + WS_CAPTION adds the caption bits twice and switches on styles you never asked for. The colour macro RGB, coming in Drawing with GDI, packs three bytes into one number with the same shifts and |.

walk: Each flag is 1 shifted left: 1u << 0 is 1. The u makes it unsigned. The brackets matter: a macro pastes text, and without them an expression around it could split the shift apart.
1u << 3 is 8, binary 1000. The four flags are 1, 2, 4 and 8, so each one owns a different bit.
| joins flags: 1 | 4 is 5, binary 0101. Alive and shielded are on; jumping and poisoned are off.
|= sets a bit: 5 | 8 is 13. The bits already on stay on.
~ flips every bit, so ~FLAG_SHIELD has every bit on except bit 2. &= with it clears just the shield: 13 becomes 9.
Prints after hit: 9: alive (1) plus poisoned (8).
The test. flags & FLAG_POISONED is 9 & 8, which is 8, not 0, so it’s true. The extra brackets are needed: without them, != would run first.
The short form: any nonzero result counts as true. 9 & 4 is 0, so shielded doesn’t print.
rungs.model: Mental model: a row of light switches on one panel. | flips chosen switches on, & ~ flips chosen switches off, and & on its own is a stencil that hides every switch except the one you want to look at.

opts: start: 5, after hit: 9, then poisoned
start: 5, after hit: 13, then poisoned and shielded
start: 5, after hit: 9, then poisoned and shielded
start: 1, after hit: 9, then poisoned
check.hint: Write the four flags as 1, 2, 4 and 8. Which are on after each line?
check.why: 1 | 4 is 5. Setting poisoned makes 13, and clearing the shield takes 4 away, leaving 9. Then 9 & 8 is 8, which is true, and 9 & 4 is 0, which is false, so only poisoned prints.

miss.1: &= ~FLAG_SHIELD clears bit 2: ~ makes a mask with every bit except the shield, and & keeps only those. 13 becomes 9.
miss.2: The values are right, but 9 & 4 is 0, and 0 is false, so shielded doesn’t print.
miss.3: That would be ||, which only gives 0 or 1. A single | combines bits: 1 | 4 is 5.

tryit.task: The player jumps: turn the jumping bit on, then print whether they are jumping.

qa: Why unsigned?
Shifting a 1 into the top bit of a signed int is undefined behaviour, and ~ on a signed value gives a negative number. Unsigned bits are just bits. Print them with %u, or %x to see them in hex.
How many flags fit?
32 in an unsigned int on MSVC, which is 4 bytes. For more, use unsigned long long and 1ull << n, which gives 64.
Why not just four int variables?

You can, and for four flags it’s fine. Flags win when there are many: you pass one value to a function, save one number to a file, and test several at once with one &. Windows takes dozens of options this way in a single DWORD.
What does ^ do?
Exclusive or: a 1 where the two sides differ. flags ^= FLAG_JUMPING flips that bit, on to off or off to on.
How do I test two flags at once?
(flags & (FLAG_ALIVE | FLAG_SHIELD)) != 0 means “either one is on”. (flags & mask) == mask means “both are on”.
rungs.bridge: You can pack and unpack flags. Next: The window procedure, where Windows hands you messages with values packed the same way.

rungs.title: The window procedure (WndProc) and messages
rungs.builds: WinMain and the window handle (the callback address you handed Windows), Function pointers (Phase 3.75), switch statements (Phase 2.5) and Combining flags with | and &.
rungs.why: Everything that happens to your window arrives here as a numbered message: a key, a click, a repaint request, the close button. Your whole game’s reaction to the outside world is a switch inside this one function.

parts: Windows calls you

The window procedure is a callback: a function you write but never call yourself. You gave Windows its address in WinMain and the window handle, and Windows calls it whenever something happens to the window. It's the same deal as qsort's compare function from Function pointers: you supply the function, someone else decides when it runs. Most calls arrive through DispatchMessage in your loop. A few come straight from Windows during another call. CreateWindowEx sends messages before it even returns, so inside WindowProc use the hwnd parameter, never g_hwnd.
Messages are numbers

Every WM_ name is a #define: WM_KEYDOWN is 0x0100, WM_PAINT is 0x000F, WM_DESTROY is 0x0002. The preprocessor swaps the names out before the compiler runs, so in The debugger's Locals panel msg shows a bare 256, not WM_KEYDOWN. It's the enum lesson from the other side. Hover over a WM_ name in VS Code to see its number when you need to match one up.
wp and lp carry the details

What wp and lp mean depends on the message. For WM_KEYDOWN, wp is the virtual-key code: VK_LEFT, VK_ESCAPE, or the capital letter itself for letter keys, so wp == 'W' works. For mouse messages, lp holds two numbers packed into one: x in the low 16 bits, y in the next 16. You unpack them with a mask and a shift, as in Combining flags with | and &:

int x = (int)(lp & 0xFFFF);
int y = (int)((lp >> 16) & 0xFFFF);

That breaks for negative positions, which happen with two monitors or when you drag outside the window: -5 comes out as 65531. windowsx.h has GET_X_LPARAM(lp) and GET_Y_LPARAM(lp), which read those 16 bits as a signed short. Use them for mouse positions.
Mistakes to watch for

• No default: that calls DefWindowProc. Then nothing handles moving, resizing or the X button, and the window seems frozen.
  • A missing break falls through into the next case, just as in switch statements.
  • Forgetting PostQuitMessage in WM_DESTROY. The window goes and the program keeps running.
MSVC notes

The function's shape has to match WNDPROC exactly: LRESULT, CALLBACK, then HWND, UINT, WPARAM, LPARAM. Get one wrong and MSVC warns on the wc.lpfnWndProc = WindowProc; line, and /WX stops the build. Fix the function, don't cast the warning away: a cast hides a mismatch that crashes later.

walk: This is the WndProc. You never call it. Windows does, with the window (hwnd), the message number (msg) and two extra values (wp, lp).
A plain switch from Phase 2.5, choosing by message number. The WM_ names are #defines for those numbers, so the debugger shows the number.
A key went down. wp says which one: here, a virtual-key code like VK_ESCAPE.
Asks Windows to tear the window down. That makes Windows send you WM_DESTROY.
On WM_DESTROY the window is going away. PostQuitMessage drops a WM_QUIT message in the queue so the loop in WinMain can stop. The message loop and PeekMessage looks at that next.
In the default case: every message you don’t handle must go to DefWindowProc. It does the standard behaviour: dragging, resizing, the X button, and so on.
Returning 0 tells Windows “handled”.
After the loop ends, wParam holds the 0 you gave PostQuitMessage. It becomes the program’s exit code.
rungs.model: Mental model: WndProc is your window’s receptionist. Every event knocks on the door with a message number. You handle the ones you care about and send everything else to Windows’ own front desk, DefWindowProc.

check.q: You delete the whole WM_DESTROY case, then run the program and click the X. What happens?
opts: The window vanishes but the program keeps running
The window refuses to close, because nothing handles the click
The program crashes with an access violation when you click X
Nothing visible changes: Windows ends the program for you
check.hint: Who tells the message loop to stop?
check.why: DefWindowProc still closes and destroys the window, so it vanishes. But nobody calls PostQuitMessage, so no quit message is ever posted and the message loop never finishes. You get an invisible program stuck in Task Manager.

miss.1: DefWindowProc handles the close button fine, so the window does go away.
miss.2: Nothing here is invalid. The program just never stops.
miss.3: Windows doesn’t end your process when your window closes. Only your own loop ending (via WM_QUIT) does that.

tryit.task: Make the program end when the window is destroyed.

qa: What are wp and lp?

Extra details whose meaning depends on the message. For WM_KEYDOWN, wp is the key. For a mouse click, lp holds the position, packed as two 16-bit halves. WPARAM and LPARAM are pointer-sized integer types.
Why return DefWindowProc in the default case?
DefWindowProc does the standard work for messages you ignore (moving, resizing, the X button) and gives back the result Windows expects. Returning your own 0 for everything would break all of that.
Why is it called WindowProc here but WndProc everywhere?
The name is yours to choose. “WndProc” is the traditional name, and the starter code calls it WindowProc. The function is the same thing.
Why does Windows call me, instead of me calling it?

A console program calls scanf and waits, so you are in charge. A window is one of many on the desktop, and Windows owns the mouse, keyboard and screen. It decides when you need a redraw or a key arrived. You hand it your WndProc once, like a phone number, and it rings whenever something happens.
Why not LOWORD and HIWORD for the mouse?
They read the halves as unsigned, so a position left of or above the window turns into a huge number. GET_X_LPARAM and GET_Y_LPARAM from windowsx.h keep the sign.
rungs.bridge: You can react to messages. Next: the message loop and PeekMessage, how messages get to WndProc, and how a game keeps running between them.

rungs.title: The message loop and PeekMessage
rungs.builds: The window procedure, The game loop: input, update, render, wait (Phase 4.5) and Copying and joining strings (Phase 3), for snprintf.
rungs.why: The loop is how your program collects its messages and hands them to WndProc. A normal app uses GetMessage and waits. A game can’t wait, because enemies must move even when nobody presses a key, so it uses PeekMessage and runs a frame whether or not a message arrived.

parts: Peek, don't wait

GetMessage waits until a message arrives, which is right for a text editor and wrong for a game. PeekMessage returns at once. Each frame, an inner while keeps calling it with PM_REMOVE until the queue is empty, handing each message to WindowProc. Then you run one frame. PeekMessage doesn't return 0 for WM_QUIT the way GetMessage does, so check msg.message == WM_QUIT yourself.
Text with snprintf

The title text comes from snprintf, from Copying and joining strings: snprintf(title, sizeof title, "Frame %d", frame);. It works like printf but writes into the array, never past sizeof title, and always ends with '\0'. Old Win32 samples use wsprintf, which has no size limit at all. Swap it for snprintf when you copy one, and include stdio.h.
The catch: dragging the window

Hold the title bar to drag the window, or grab an edge to resize it, and the frame counter stops. DefWindowProc runs a loop of its own inside that DispatchMessage call until you let go of the mouse, so your loop is stuck in one call. The menu bar does the same. It's normal; a game just pauses. There are fixes, but you don't need them yet.
MSVC notes
snprintf builds clean under /W4 /WX; your test build confirmed it. sprintf and wsprintf don't check the size, and MSVC flags sprintf with C4996, as it did strcpy.

walk: A MSG struct (Phase 3.5) that each message is copied into. Zeroed so it’s safe to read at the end.
The outer loop is your game loop from Phase 4.5: one pass per frame.

PeekMessage asks “anything waiting?”. It returns right away: nonzero if there was a message (copied into msg and removed, thanks to PM_REMOVE), 0 if the queue was empty. This inner loop empties the queue each frame.

msg.message is the message number (WM_QUIT, WM_KEYDOWN, and so on). Unlike GetMessage, PeekMessage does not return 0 for WM_QUIT. It hands it over like any message, so you must check for it and stop yourself.
Sends the message to the right window’s WindowProc. This is the moment Windows calls your function. TranslateMessage just turns raw key presses into character messages.
The queue is empty, so run the frame: update and draw. Here the “game” just counts frames.
snprintf, from Copying and joining strings: like printf, but writes “Frame 1”, “Frame 2”… into title, never more than sizeof title bytes. That’s why stdio.h is on line 2.
Puts that text in the window’s title bar, so you can watch the loop run.
Without this the loop would spin as fast as it can and use a whole CPU core. Frame time replaces this guess with real timing.
rungs.model: Mental model: GetMessage is standing at the post office until a letter arrives. PeekMessage is glancing in the mailbox on your way past: letter or no letter, you carry on with your day. A game needs the glance.

check.q: You delete the line if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = 0; and run the program. You click the X. What happens?
opts: The window closes and the program exits as normal, as it did before
The program crashes because WM_QUIT is never handled anywhere
PeekMessage returns 0 forever, so the title stops changing
The window goes, but the loop carries on counting frames
check.hint: With GetMessage, WM_QUIT makes the call return 0. Does PeekMessage do that?
check.why: The X button leads to WM_DESTROY, then PostQuitMessage puts WM_QUIT in the queue. PeekMessage just returns it like any message, so only your own check can end the loop. Without it, running stays 1 and the outer loop never stops.

miss.0: Nothing else sets running to 0. The loop only ends because of that line.
miss.1: An unhandled message isn’t a crash. DispatchMessage with WM_QUIT does nothing harmful.
miss.2: PeekMessage returns 0 when the queue is empty, which is how the inner loop ends each frame. It doesn’t stop the outer loop.

tryit.task: Fill in the PeekMessage call so it checks any window, any message, and removes what it finds.

qa: When would I use GetMessage instead?
For a normal app (editor, calculator) that only needs to do something when an event arrives. It sleeps until then, which uses no CPU. Games use PeekMessage.
Why is the inner loop a while, not an if?
Several messages can pile up between frames. A while handles all of them before you draw. An if would handle one per frame and the input would lag.
Why does Windows say “Not Responding”?
If you stop pulling messages for a few seconds, Windows assumes you’ve frozen. A slow frame or a missing loop causes it.
How does this compare to my Phase 2.5 and 4.5 loops?
It is the same shape. GetMessage is waiting like scanf, PeekMessage is checking without waiting like _kbhit, and WndProc is the “react to it” step. The job is still read input, update, draw.
Why snprintf and not wsprintf?
wsprintf is an old Windows function with no size limit, so a long string runs straight past the end of the array. snprintf is standard C, takes the size, and you already know it.
rungs.bridge: You can explain how messages flow. Next: drawing with GDI and InvalidateRect, putting a coloured rectangle on screen.

rungs.title: Drawing with GDI and InvalidateRect
rungs.builds: The window procedure, The message loop and PeekMessage, and Combining flags with | and & (RGB packs bytes the same way).
rungs.why: In a window you don’t print. You draw when Windows asks you to, inside WM_PAINT. To move something you change your variables, then tell Windows “this is out of date, ask me to redraw”. That’s InvalidateRect. This concept gets you the coloured rectangle and the arrow keys.

parts: Draw when asked

You only draw inside WM_PAINT, between BeginPaint and EndPaint. To move something, change your variables and call InvalidateRect, which marks the window out of date. Windows sends WM_PAINT once the queue has nothing more urgent, and several InvalidateRect calls in a row become one repaint.
y grows downward

(0, 0) is the top-left corner of the client area, the part inside the border. x grows to the right and y grows down, so the up arrow subtracts from y. A RECT holds left, top, right and bottom, and FillRect stops just short of right and bottom: a RECT from 100 to 150 is 50 pixels wide.
RGB packs three bytes

RGB is a macro with parameters, like the #defines from Named constants with #define but taking arguments. Simplified, RGB(r, g, b) becomes r | (g << 8) | (b << 16): three bytes in one number, built the way Combining flags with | and & built flags. Red sits in the lowest byte, so RGB(0, 200, 100) is 0x0064C800, and the hex reads blue, green, red. A web colour #FF8800 is RGB(0xFF, 0x88, 0x00), not 0xFF8800. Each argument is cut to one byte, so RGB(300, 0, 0) quietly gives 44.
A number dressed as a brush

FillRect wants an HBRUSH. (HBRUSH)(COLOR_WINDOW + 1) casts a small number to a handle type. FillRect is written to spot small values and treat them as “this system colour”. The +1 is there because COLOR_SCROLLBAR is 0, and 0 would look like NULL. It's a trick that only works for these functions. Don't DeleteObject it: you never created it. A brush from CreateSolidBrush is yours, so delete it when you're done.
Braces after case WM_PAINT:

In C17 a case label must be followed by a statement, and a declaration like PAINTSTRUCT ps; isn't one. The braces make a block, which is a statement. They also keep ps and hdc inside this case, so no other case can use them by mistake. C23 relaxes the rule, and MSVC already accepts the brace-less form even with /std:c17, so you will see code without them. Keep the braces anyway: gcc in C17 mode rejects that code, and the braces keep ps and hdc in their own case.
Mistakes to watch for

• Drawing in WM_KEYDOWN. The next repaint wipes it.
  • Skipping BeginPaint in WM_PAINT. BeginPaint is what marks the window as painted; without it Windows sends WM_PAINT again and again. Every BeginPaint also needs its EndPaint, which hands the drawing surface back.
  • Forgetting DeleteObject. Each process gets about 10,000 GDI objects; leak one per frame and drawing stops working within minutes.

walk: The rectangle’s position lives in plain variables, like the player x in your console game.
Arrow keys arrive here. Change the position only, no drawing yet. Up and down are your tryit; remember y grows downward.
“This window’s picture is out of date.” Windows answers later by sending WM_PAINT. NULL means the whole window, TRUE means erase the background first.
The one place you draw. Windows sends it on first show, after the window is uncovered or restored, and after InvalidateRect. The { } after the case are needed because you declare variables inside it.
A struct (Phase 3.5) that Windows fills in when painting starts. Its rcPaint field is the area that needs repainting.
Starts drawing and gives you hdc, a “device context”: the thing you draw onto. EndPaint must follow.

Clears the area to the window colour first. (HBRUSH)(COLOR_WINDOW + 1) is the standard way to ask for “the normal window colour” as a brush. Without this clear, the old rectangle stays behind and you smear.
A RECT holds left, top, right, bottom. SetRect fills them in: a 50 by 50 square at the current position.
A brush is a colour you paint with. RGB(0, 200, 100) packs red, green and blue into one number: green. CreateSolidBrush lives in gdi32.lib (Linking libraries).
You made the brush, so you delete it. Forget this and Windows slowly runs out of GDI objects.
rungs.model: Mental model: your variables are the truth, the window is a painting of them. Changing a variable doesn’t change the painting. InvalidateRect is the “wet paint, redo me” sign, and WM_PAINT is you redoing it from the variables.

check.q: You delete the InvalidateRect line and press the right arrow a few times. What do you see?
opts: The rectangle moves exactly as before, since the variable still changes
It does not move until a repaint is forced, such as minimise and restore
The program crashes inside WM_PAINT because nothing was invalidated
The rectangle jumps to the far right edge of the window at once
check.hint: Does changing g_rect_x draw anything by itself?
check.why: g_rect_x does change, but nothing asks Windows to repaint, so WM_PAINT isn’t sent and the screen still shows the old picture. Minimise and restore the window and WM_PAINT fires and the rectangle suddenly appears at its new place.

miss.0: The variable changes, but drawing only happens in WM_PAINT, and nothing triggers it.
miss.2: Nothing is invalid. WM_PAINT simply doesn’t run.
miss.3: The position still changes by 5 per key press. It just isn’t drawn.

tryit.task: Add the up arrow so it moves the rectangle up.

qa: Why is there flicker?
FillRect clears the real window, then the rectangle is drawn on top, and the user can catch the in-between. Double buffering, at the end of this phase, fixes it.
What does the TRUE do in InvalidateRect?
It asks Windows to erase the background first. This class has no background brush, so the FillRect in WM_PAINT does the clearing. Pass FALSE if you only want the repaint.
Why not draw straight in WM_KEYDOWN?
Windows can ask for a repaint at any time (another window moved away). If drawing only happens on key presses, those repaints show garbage. One place, WM_PAINT, always draws from the variables.
Why is RGB backwards in hex?
Windows puts red in the lowest byte. Hex is written with the highest byte first, so you read blue, green, red. Always build colours with RGB() and the order looks after itself.
rungs.bridge: You can draw and move a rectangle. Next: Frame time, measuring how long each frame really takes.

rungs.title: Frame time (QueryPerformanceCounter)
rungs.builds: Frame timing with Sleep (Phase 4.5), Division, remainder and casts (Phase 2), and The message loop and PeekMessage.
rungs.why: Sleep(16) asks for a wait of about 16 ms, but the real wait varies and the frame’s own work adds more. To move things at the same speed on every PC, and to know how fast your loop really runs, you measure each frame with a high-resolution timer.

parts: A stopwatch that counts ticks

QueryPerformanceCounter reads a counter that ticks millions of times a second. QueryPerformanceFrequency tells you how many ticks make a second: 10,000,000 on most Windows 10 and 11 PCs, but always ask. A single reading means nothing. Two readings, subtracted and divided by the frequency, give the seconds between them.
LARGE_INTEGER is a union

Both functions fill in a LARGE_INTEGER. It's a union: like a struct, except every member shares the same bytes. Simplified from winnt.h:

typedef union {
    struct { DWORD LowPart; LONG HighPart; } u;
    LONGLONG QuadPart;
} LARGE_INTEGER;

That's two views of one 8-byte value: the whole 64-bit number, or its two 32-bit halves. The halves are from before compilers had 64-bit integers. x64 is little-endian, storing the lowest byte first, so LowPart is the bottom 32 bits of QuadPart. You use QuadPart.
Reading the other member

King warns that after writing one member, reading a different member gives you a meaningless value. That was the C89 view. Since the corrections to C99, the standard says you get the same bytes read as the other type, which is exactly how Windows uses LARGE_INTEGER. MSVC has always worked that way.
Subtract first, then convert

now.QuadPart - last.QuadPart is exact integer maths, and the answer is small. Cast that to double, multiply by 1000 and divide by the frequency. Don't convert each reading first: a float holds about 7 digits and a counter reading has 13 or more, so the difference comes out as junk. And cast before you divide, or Division, remainder and casts happens again and you only get whole milliseconds.
Sleep and 60 fps

Sleep wakes on Windows' timer tick, about 15.6 ms by default, so Sleep(16) often lasts 31 ms. timeBeginPeriod(1) (timeapi.h, linked with winmm.lib) asks for 1 ms ticks; call timeEndPeriod(1) before you exit. Since Windows 10 version 2004 that setting only affects your own program. Before, any program could change it for everyone, so a game seemed smooth only while a browser was open. To hold 60 fps, measure the frame, then sleep for what's left of 16.67 ms. If the frame ran long, skip the Sleep: a negative wait turned into a DWORD is huge, as Frame timing with Sleep showed.
MSVC notes

freopen gets MSVC's C4996 "unsafe" warning, like scanf did, so line 1 defines _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS before any include. If build.bat also passes /D_CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS, delete the line, or you get C4005 for defining it twice.

walk: MSVC calls freopen unsafe (warning C4996, which /WX turns into an error). This line, placed before the includes, turns that off.
A windowed program has no console by default, so printf shows nothing. AllocConsole opens one, and freopen points stdout at it. Plumbing: copy it as is.
A LARGE_INTEGER is a union: one 8-byte value you can read whole (.QuadPart) or as two halves. freq is ticks per second (it depends on the PC); last and now are readings.
Fills in freq once. It never changes while the program runs.
The first reading: the stopwatch starts here. The number itself means nothing, only the difference between two readings does.
The old guess. Now we measure what it really did.

Subtract the two readings as integers first, then convert the small difference to double, times 1000 for milliseconds, divided by ticks per second. Casting first means the division isn’t whole-number division.
The end of this frame is the start of the next one.
rungs.model: Mental model: a stopwatch you press at the end of every lap. You don’t trust that the lap was “about 16 ms”. You read the stopwatch, write it down, and press it again.

check.q: On a typical Windows PC, with the default timer settings, roughly what does this program print each frame?
opts: Exactly 16.0 ms on every line, because that is what Sleep was told
Roughly 16 to 32 ms, varying a little line to line
About 1 ms on every line, since the loop itself does almost no work
About 60 on every line, because 1000 divided by 16 is roughly 60
check.hint: Sleep(16) is a request, not a promise. And the number printed is milliseconds, not frames.
check.why: Sleep wakes on Windows’ timer ticks (about 15.6 ms by default), so Sleep(16) often lands on a steady ~31 ms, or ~16–17 ms if the timer resolution has been raised. The measured value includes that, plus message handling, and wobbles. That wobble is the whole reason to measure.

miss.0: Sleep isn’t exact. The timer ticks about every 15.6 ms, so the real wait varies.
miss.2: The loop itself is fast, but Sleep(16) still waits about 16 ms or more each frame.
miss.3: That’s frames per second, and the program prints milliseconds per frame. 60 would be an fps, not an ms.

tryit.task: Turn ms into seconds (dt), the number you multiply speeds by.

qa: Why not just GetTickCount?

It only counts whole milliseconds and updates on the same coarse timer tick, so it’s too jumpy for 60 fps frame timing. QueryPerformanceCounter has a resolution well under a microsecond (typically 100 ns).
How do I hold 60 fps properly?
Compare the frame time to a target of about 16.67 ms and only Sleep for what’s left, instead of a fixed Sleep(16). Skip the Sleep if nothing is left. That’s the task in the Phase 5 build spec.
What is dt?
Delta time: how long the last frame took, in seconds. Move by speed * dt and the game runs the same on a slow and a fast PC.
Does timeBeginPeriod drain the battery?
A little, because the PC wakes more often. That’s why you call timeEndPeriod when the game closes. Since Windows 11, Windows may also ignore the request while your window is minimised or hidden.
rungs.bridge: You can measure your loop. Next: double buffering, ending the flicker.

rungs.title: Double buffering
rungs.builds: The frame buffer (Phase 4.5), Drawing with GDI and InvalidateRect, and Static locals and globals (Phase 3).
rungs.why: Drawing straight to the window means the user can catch the half-drawn frame: cleared, but the rectangle not yet there. That’s flicker. Draw the whole frame somewhere hidden, then copy it to the window in one step. It’s your Phase 4.5 frame buffer, made of pixels.

parts: Draw behind the curtain

Make a hidden drawing surface the size of the window, draw the whole frame on it, then copy it to the window with one BitBlt. The user only ever sees finished frames. It's the frame buffer from Phase 4.5, made of pixels.
HGDIOBJ is void *

SelectObject puts a bitmap, brush or pen into a DC and hands back whatever was there before. One function serves every kind, so it takes and returns HGDIOBJ, which is a typedef for void *: a pointer to anything. In C an HBITMAP converts to and from it without a cast. Keep the old object and select it back before you delete yours. Windows won't delete a bitmap that's still selected.
Create the back buffer once

The program here builds a new bitmap on every paint, to stay short. Real code keeps it in static locals, which keep their value between calls and start at zero (Static locals and globals):

static HDC back = NULL;
static HBITMAP bmp = NULL;
static HGDIOBJ old = NULL;
static int bw = 0, bh = 0;
if (back == NULL || w != bw || h != bh) {
    if (back != NULL) { SelectObject(back, old); DeleteObject(bmp); DeleteDC(back); }
    back = CreateCompatibleDC(hdc);
    bmp = CreateCompatibleBitmap(hdc, w, h);
    old = SelectObject(back, bmp);
    bw = w; bh = h;
}

Now it's only rebuilt when the window changes size.
Mistakes to watch for

• Forgetting the deletes. A leak on every paint uses up the 10,000-object limit fast.
  • Setting hbrBackground: Windows erases the window before WM_PAINT and the flicker comes back.

walk: Asks Windows for the drawable size. It fills your RECT through the pointer (the & from Phase 3.5). rc.right and rc.bottom are the width and height.
Makes a second device context, back, that is not attached to the screen. Think of it as an off-screen drawing surface.
The actual pixels for the hidden canvas, same size and format as the window.

Puts the bitmap into the off-screen DC so drawing on back goes into it. It hands back the previous object as an HGDIOBJ, a typedef for void * that can hold any GDI handle, so you can put it back later.
Same clear as before, but onto back. Nothing here touches the screen yet.
Same rectangle, also drawn on back. The whole frame is now built off-screen.
The only drawing line that touches the visible window: copy the finished picture across in one go. SRCCOPY means “copy exactly”.
Puts the original object back into the DC. A bitmap that is still selected can’t be deleted.
Delete the bitmap (line 33) and the DC (line 34), because you made them. Skipping this leaks GDI objects every frame.
rungs.model: Mental model: a painter who sets up the whole scene behind a curtain, then pulls the curtain back. The audience never sees half-finished work (the curtain is the off-screen bitmap).

check.q: In this program, you delete the BitBlt line and leave everything else. What do you see?
opts: The same green rectangle as before, but now with no flicker at all
The rectangle drawn directly on the window, flickering as before
A compile error, because the variable back is never used anywhere
No rectangle: it was all drawn on the bitmap and never copied over
check.hint: Which line moves pixels from the hidden bitmap to the window?
check.why: All the FillRect calls draw into back, an off-screen bitmap. BitBlt is the only thing that copies it to hdc, the real window. Without it, the window never gets the picture.

miss.0: The picture never reaches the window, so there’s nothing to be flicker-free.
miss.1: The drawing no longer targets the window at all. Only BitBlt does that.
miss.2: back is used (by FillRect and SelectObject), so it compiles fine. It just never gets shown.

tryit.task: Fill in what you copy from, so the finished frame lands on the window.

qa: Why does it still flicker a tiny bit sometimes?

It shouldn’t here. The class has no background brush, so Windows erases nothing, and BitBlt replaces every pixel in one go. If you later set hbrBackground, Windows erases before WM_PAINT and flicker returns. Then return 1 from WM_ERASEBKGND, or pass FALSE to InvalidateRect.
Isn’t creating a bitmap every frame wasteful?
Yes. The Learn it part shows the real way: keep the DC and bitmap in static locals and rebuild them only when the window size changes.
Is this the same as the runner’s char array?
Same idea, different material. Build the whole frame in a buffer in memory, then put it on screen in one operation.
rungs.bridge: That’s every concept in Phase 5. Next: the prototype build, putting all of this into your own game.
